title: Workshop safety and occupational health
summary: Safe workshop practice includes accident prevention, appropriate personal protective equipment, first aid, fire protection and workplace hygiene. Identify hazards before starting and know how to act in an emergency.
points: Hazards and accident prevention

Before work, inspect tools and machines, secure the workpiece and keep the area tidy. Hazards include sharp edges, moving parts, flying chips, wood dust, noise, chemicals, slipping and material handling. Apply safety rules to the particular operation. (pp. 6, 10–11)
Personal protection and hygiene

Safety glasses protect against flying particles, hearing protection reduces noise exposure and suitable respiratory protection limits dust inhalation. Provide adequate lighting, ventilation and dust extraction. Loose clothing and unsuitable gloves must not approach rotating tools. (pp. 10–11)
First aid

Make the scene safe, check responsiveness and normal breathing, call 155 (or 112) and follow the dispatcher. If unconscious and not breathing normally, begin chest compressions and use an AED if available. Apply direct pressure for severe bleeding; avoid unnecessary movement of fractures. Some older instructions in the textbook are outdated. (pp. 7–8)
Integrated rescue system

The core Czech integrated rescue services are firefighters, emergency medical services and national police; firefighters generally coordinate joint operations. Call 150 for fire, 155 for ambulance, 158 for police, 156 for municipal police or 112 for the European emergency number. State who you are, what happened and where. (pp. 9–10)
Fire classes

A: solid materials (wood, paper); B: flammable liquids (varnish, petrol); C: gases; D: metals; F: cooking oils and fats. Choose the extinguisher according to its markings. Ordinary water or foam extinguishers are unsuitable for live electrical equipment; CO₂ may cause cold burns and forceful discharge can disturb combustible dust. (pp. 12–14)
Fire prevention

Remove accumulated wood dust, separate combustible materials from ignition sources and learn the escape routes and extinguisher locations. Fight only a small incipient fire if doing so is safe, and ensure that emergency services are alerted. (pp. 12–15)
facts: Sharp tools, rotating machinery, chips, dust, noise, heavy loads, fire and electricity.
Safety glasses, hearing protection, dust-rated respirator, appropriate footwear and clothing selected for the risk.
150 fire; 155 ambulance; 158 national police; 156 municipal police; 112 European emergency number.
Firefighters, emergency medical services and national police, with other agencies supporting as necessary.
A solids; B liquids; C gases; D metals; F cooking oils and fats. Match extinguishing agent to the marked class.
Ensure safety, assess responsiveness and normal breathing, call 155, follow instructions and start CPR if not breathing normally.
red: UPDATED INFORMATION: As of 2026, Government Regulation 495/2001 on personal protective equipment has been replaced by Regulation 390/2021; Decree 410/2005 on school hygiene by Decree 160/2024. Check current official rules.

UPDATED INFORMATION: For adults not breathing normally, current guidance recommends 100–120 chest compressions per minute, 5–6 cm deep, calling 155 and following the operator, and using an AED if available. Some older instructions in the textbook are outdated.

UPDATED INFORMATION: Do not automatically place an unconscious but normally breathing person on their back with raised legs. Monitor breathing and follow emergency service instructions; control major bleeding with direct pressure.

title: Machining
summary: Machining changes a material's shape or dimensions by removing material with a tool. The removed material is called a chip; the operation is mechanical because the wood remains wood.
points: What changes during machining
A cutting tool removes material from a workpiece to alter its length, width, thickness or profile, or to create holes. The removed portion is called a chip or shaving. (p. 16)
Types of operation
Sawing separates pieces; milling creates surfaces and profiles; drilling makes holes; mortising creates recesses; turning makes rotational shapes; sanding removes fine surface particles. (p. 16)
Relation to technology
Machining is a mechanical process, not a change to the chemical composition of wood. Choose the process according to the required shape, surface quality and accuracy. (p. 16)
facts: Progressive material removal by a cutting tool, called chip-forming machining.
Sawing, milling, drilling, mortising, turning and sanding.
Changes to the workpiece's dimensions or shape, not its chemical composition.

title: Manufacturing technology
summary: Technology describes the method used to manufacture a product. A technological procedure defines the correct sequence of tasks and may combine hand and machine work.
points: Mechanical and chemical technologies

Mechanical processes change the shape or arrangement of wood, such as converting logs into lumber and manufacturing furniture. Chemical technologies are covered only to a limited extent in joinery; their products include adhesives, coatings, paper and PUR foams. (p. 16)
Technological procedure
A procedure sets out how to make a component, semi-finished item or complete product and which operations must precede others to avoid spoiling previous work. (p. 16)
Hand and machine production

A process may be manual, machine-based or a combination. One illustrative sequence is selecting and marking material → machining parts → making and assembling joints → surface finishing. This is an example, not a universal process plan. (p. 16)
facts: Mechanical: machining and shaping. Chemical: producing or modifying substances such as adhesives and finishes.
A logically ordered sequence of operations for manufacturing a part or product.
Measuring, machining, assembly and finishing must be arranged appropriately.

title: The joiner's workplace
summary: A joiner's workshop needs adequate space, suitable environmental conditions and order. Its central bench is a woodworking workbench used to hold workpieces securely.
points: Workshop
The work area must satisfy spatial, thermal and hygiene requirements. Keeping the shop orderly and wearing appropriate working clothes and footwear directly improve safety and workmanship. (p. 18)
Workbench construction

A traditional woodworking bench has a robust top with a tool trough and an underframe. A front vice is usually on the left and an end vice on the right; steel screws operate the clamping mechanisms. (p. 18)
Bench dogs and protection
Adjustable bench dogs help secure longer pieces. Use a suitable backing board when drilling, mortising and gluing to avoid damaging the workbench surface. (p. 18)
facts: Top, underframe, tool trough, front and end vices, steel screws and bench dogs.
Height-adjustable stops used for holding longer workpieces.
Use a backing board for drilling, mortising and glue-ups.
A basic element of safety, efficiency and health protection.

title: Measuring and marking tools
summary: Accurate measurement and marking precede machining. Length and thickness are checked with rules, tapes and callipers; angles with squares and bevel gauges; layout lines with a pencil and marking gauge.
points: Measuring versus marking

Measuring determines length, width, thickness or an angle using a measuring tool. Marking transfers a required measurement onto the workpiece using a pencil or awl; the line identifies where to cut. (p. 19)
Rules, tapes and precision

Folding rules are usually 1–2 m long; retractable tape measures contain a steel strip, and long tapes serve larger distances. For fine measurements the book warns against relying on a worn tape hook. One inch equals 25.4 mm; the book quotes 1 mm as normal furniture-making accuracy. (pp. 19–20)
Vernier calliper

The outer and inner jaws measure external and internal dimensions, and the depth rod measures holes. Read whole millimetres on the main scale and tenths at the aligned vernier graduation. The book illustrates 15.8 mm. Protect the jaws from drops and impacts. (pp. 21–23)
Checking angles

A try square checks 90° and can be tested by comparison with another accurate square. A fixed mitre square checks 45°, an adjustable bevel gauge transfers other angles and a protractor measures them. (pp. 23–24)
Level and plumb
A spirit level uses a bubble vial to check horizontal and often vertical surfaces. A plumb bob checks vertical alignment; laser measuring tools can replace some of these applications. (p. 25)
Marking wood

A sharp, relatively hard pencil produces a narrow line; a broad carpenter's pencil is less suitable for accurate joinery. A marking gauge scribes lines parallel to a reference edge, while dividers mark circles and arcs. (pp. 26–27)
facts: Folding rule, tape measure, long measuring tape, calliper, outside and inside callipers.
Measures outside and inside dimensions and depth; main scale and vernier (0.1 mm in the textbook).
Try square 90°; fixed mitre square 45°; adjustable bevel gauge transfers other angles.
Spirit level with vial, plumb bob or laser devices.
Scribes a line at a set distance parallel to a reference edge.
1 inch = 25.4 mm; the textbook specifies ordinary furniture-making measurement to 1 mm.

title: Sawing and hand saws
summary: A saw removes wood using a toothed blade. Tooth size, tooth geometry, cutting direction and guidance determine cutting speed and quality. Maintenance and safe handling are essential.
points: Teeth and cut quality
Coarse teeth remove material faster but leave a rougher surface; fine teeth cut more slowly and cleanly. Tooth geometry is selected for cutting along or across the wood grain. (p. 28)
Frame saws

A coarse rip/crosscut frame saw is often over 700 mm long. A fine tenon-type frame saw is about 600–700 mm long for accurate tenons and dovetails. A narrow-bladed turning saw, up to about 10 mm wide, cuts curves. Check blade tension and twist before work. (pp. 28–29)
Backless and specialist hand saws

A tenon saw has a short, wide, fine-toothed blade; a panel saw is for larger pieces; a keyhole saw cuts internal openings; a grooving saw cuts sliding-dovetail grooves; a fret saw cuts delicate shapes; a veneer saw cuts veneer against a straightedge. Traditional Japanese saws generally cut on the pull stroke. (pp. 30–32)
Correct sawing technique

A conventional frame saw usually cuts on the forward stroke. Start with short, light strokes; once the kerf forms, use the blade's full length without excessive pressure. Slow down at the exit to avoid splintering. The textbook cautions about keeping the guiding thumb clear. (p. 33)
Maintenance and terminology

The tooth line joins the tooth tips, which should have equal height. The face is the cutting-facing surface, the back is behind it, and pitch is the distance between tips. Setting teeth alternately creates a kerf wider than the blade to prevent binding. Hardened modern teeth may not be sharpenable with ordinary files. (pp. 35–36)
facts: Frame saws and handle-mounted hand saws.
Coarse saw for rough cuts; fine frame saw for tenons; turning saw for curves.
Tenon, panel, keyhole, grooving, fret and veneer saws.
Usually cut when pulled and typically use a thin blade.
The alignment of tooth tips; uniform height matters.
Alternately bent teeth make a wider kerf and reduce binding.
Secure the workpiece, keep blade straight, avoid forcing the cut and finish carefully.

title: Planing and hand planes
summary: Planing removes long shavings to create flat or profiled wood surfaces. Different planes serve different tasks and require a sharp, accurately adjusted iron.
points: Principle and components
A wooden plane has a body, sole, blade bed, mouth for shavings, wedge and handles. The iron has a face, back, cutting edge and bevel. (pp. 37–38)
Adjusting the iron

How far the cutting edge projects below the sole controls shaving thickness. A cap iron, screwed to the blade, bends shavings close to the cutting edge and reduces tear-out. The textbook gives about 1 mm between cap iron and edge and an edge angle of around 25°. (p. 38)
Four main plane types

The scrub plane (about 250 × 33 mm) has a rounded iron for rapid rough removal. The smoothing plane (about 250 × 48 mm) levels a surface, including end grain. The cap-iron plane (about 250 × 48 mm) produces a cleaner surface. The narrow rebate plane (about 20–40 mm wide) works grooves and profiles. (pp. 39–40)
Special planes

A jointer plane is longer for flattening large work; a toothing plane roughens surfaces; a fine finishing plane produces the final surface; special grooving and curved-body planes make shaped parts. Metal planes and Japanese pull planes are also available. (p. 41)
Planing sequence

Clamp the workpiece; the textbook recommends orienting its bark-facing side toward the workbench. Select and set the plane, work with the grain and check flatness with one straightedge or two matching winding sticks. Set thickness and width with a marking gauge referenced to an already true face. (p. 42)
Grinding and honing

Grind a bevel (the book illustrates 25–30°) and remove the burr by honing on an appropriate stone, using suitable lubricant. Start coarser and finish finer. High-speed grinding may overheat and soften the blade; use light pressure, cooling and eye protection. (pp. 43–44)
Cabinet scraper and storage

A cabinet scraper is a thin steel plate for delicate finishing, curved areas and veneered surfaces. Unlike a plane iron it cuts with a deliberately raised burr. Never set a plane down directly on its projecting blade or damage may occur. (pp. 41, 47–48)
facts: Body, sole, bed, mouth, iron, wedge, handle and adjustment elements.
Face, back, cutting edge and bevel; commonly about 25–30° sharpening bevel depending on tool.
Breaks shavings near the cutting edge to reduce tear-out.
Scrub: heavy removal; smoothing: levelling; cap-iron: clean finish; rebate: grooves and profiles.
Jointer, fine finishing and toothing planes, grooving and shaped planes.
Secure the workpiece, check grain and iron setting, plane with the grain, verify flatness.
Grind bevel, hone away burr, use suitable stone lubricant and maintain stone flatness.
Steel scraper with a raised working burr for delicate surface finishing.

title: Mortising and chisels
summary: Chiselling removes wood chips to produce mortises, grooves and shaped recesses. Select chisel width and shape for the joint; maintain a sharp edge and work safely.
points: Purpose of mortising
Use chisels to remove chips and make mortises, grooves, dovetail sockets or curved recesses. Secure the workpiece and match chisel width to the intended joint. (pp. 49–50)
Bench chisel and its parts

A flat bench chisel is the most common type. The book lists widths 6, 8, 10, 12, 14 mm and beyond. Its parts are blade, bevel, neck, shoulder and handle; a metal ferrule protects the handle from mallet blows. (p. 49)
Gouges and mortise chisels

Curved gouges carve rounded shapes and recesses, about 1–60 mm wide in the textbook. Mortise chisels have a much thicker blade for deep mortises and are listed in approximately 4–14 mm widths. (pp. 50–51)
Maintenance and safety

Sharpen and hone chisels much like plane irons, avoiding heat that would soften steel. Strike with a wooden joiner's mallet; never direct the cutting edge toward your hand or body and put chisels down with the edge facing away. (pp. 51–52)
facts: General work on mortises, grooves and sockets; various blade widths.
Thick, rigid blade for narrow/deep mortises.
Curved shapes and hardware recesses; carving.
Bevel, blade, neck, shoulder and handle.
Usually beechwood; protects the handle from damage.
Never chisel toward your hand or body; store edges facing away.

title: Drilling and drilling tools
summary: Drilling forms cylindrical holes with a rotating cutting tool. Drill types vary in guidance, grain cutting, chip removal and possible hole size.
points: Drill construction
A centre point locates the hole, spurs sever fibres cleanly around the edge and spiral flutes remove chips from the hole. (pp. 53–55)
Manual tools

An awl marks a hole location or starts a small screw hole. A gimlet drills by hand. Traditional spoon or centre bits have a threaded tip, cutting spurs and a broad cutter and were used with a brace; adjustable forms also exist. (pp. 53–54)
Auger and spade bits

An auger bit has a spiral for clearing chips and works in hard and end-grain wood; the textbook lists sizes from roughly 8 mm. A flat spade bit is a simple tool for larger holes and can be used in an electric drill. (pp. 54–55)
Brad-point and Forstner bits

A woodworking twist bit has a centre point and spurs unlike a standard metalworking drill, providing straighter, cleaner holes. A Forstner bit uses rim cutters and broad cutting lips for large accurate flat-bottomed holes; securely clamp the work and preferably use a drill press because of torque. (pp. 55–56)
Countersinks, care and hazards
A countersink makes a recess for a screw head. Protect the cutting edges and do not use wood bits to drill metal. A large bit that jams can violently rotate an unsecured workpiece. (pp. 56–57)
facts: Awl, gimlet, centre bit, auger bit, spade bit, brad-point bit, Forstner bit and countersink.
Guides the drill and reduces wandering along the grain.
Score the hole perimeter to prevent torn fibres.
Deep holes with efficient chip removal through a spiral.
Wide, accurate flat-bottom holes, often for furniture fittings.
Recess for a countersunk screw head.
Clamp the workpiece firmly; a jammed bit can spin it.

title: Filing and rasping
summary: Files and rasps shape edges, curves and transitions. Their main differences are tooth form, coarseness and removal rate.
points: Construction
Files and rasps have a hard toothed body and a pointed tang held in a handle. Tool length excludes the tang; tools differ in length, section and tooth pattern. (p. 58)
Files

Files have finer teeth and different sections: flat, half-round, round or triangular. Single-cut teeth are parallel, double-cut teeth cross. Joinery often uses a half-round single-cut file; needle files serve delicate work. (pp. 58–59)
Rasps
Rasps have prominent individual teeth for faster wood removal but can tear fibres. The book highlights the half-round rasp. Coarseness depends on tooth size and spacing. (p. 59)
Handling

Always clamp the work, use a handle and guide the tool with both hands, moving slightly sideways on curves. Files are hardened and brittle: never use them as levers. Clean clogged teeth with a suitable brush and avoid impacts against other tools. (pp. 59–60)
facts: Fine cut in several sections, selected for wood, metal or plastic.
Coarse individual teeth, higher wood removal rate, may tear grain.
Single and double cut; teeth may be cut or milled.
Secure the workpiece, use a handle, guide evenly without excessive pressure.
Brush out clogged teeth; protect brittle tools from impacts and never lever with them.
